finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: user-supplied query parameter q is interpolated into an f-string SQL statement with no escaping or binding, letting an unauthenticated attacker read arbitrary data from shop.db via UNION-based injection.
finding.sink: app.py:12 db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'")

trace.note: Route /search is registered with no auth decorator or check
term taken directly from request.args q, default empty string
term concatenated into SQL text via f-string; no escaping or parameter binding
fetchall executes the injected SQL on sqlite connection db (app.py:6)
result rows returned as JSON to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: No validation, allowlist, escaping, length limit, or parameter binding on the path from q to the SQL string. A single quote breaks out of the LIKE literal; sqlite3 execute rejects stacked statements, so impact is read-only disclosure (e.g., UNION SELECT from sqlite_master and any other table). Routes /product/<int:pid> (app.py:16-19) and /by-owner (app.py:22-26) use ? parameter binding and were judged SAFE for injection. Fix: db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE ?", (f"%{term}%",)).

verdict.guard_found: none. /search (app.py:9-10) has no auth decorator or check. q is read raw at app.py:11 and f-string-interpolated into the SQL text at app.py:12 with no escaping, allowlist, length limit, or parameter binding. The "?" binding at app.py:18 and app.py:25 is on other routes and does not cover /search. The sqlite3 single-statement restriction blocks stacked queries but not UNION SELECT, so the claimed read-only disclosure still works.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: the unauthenticated route at app.py:9-10 takes q from request.args at app.py:11 and concatenates it into the SQL string at app.py:12 with no guard in between, so an anonymous attacker can break out of the LIKE literal and use UNION SELECT to read other tables such as sqlite_master.
